Treat the two equivalences as logical packaging: all four component statements are independently true, so each implication may ignore its hypothesis.

Organize the argument around these standard facts:

1. For any set \(s\) in a real vector space, \(s\subseteq\{x\mid \operatorname{gauge}_s(x)\le 1\}\), using \(1\) (or values approaching \(1\)) in the defining infimum of the gauge.

2. For a seminorm \(p\), prove by function extensionality that
   \[
   \operatorname{gauge}(\operatorname{ball}_p(0,1))(x)=p(x).
   \]
   The key representation is
   \[
   x\in r\cdot\operatorname{ball}_p(0,1)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p(x)<r
   \]
   for \(r>0\), so the relevant infimum is \(p(x)\).

3. Unfold the smoothing construction into its sequence of normalized powers. The hypothesis
   \[
   \mu(x^n)=\mu(x)^n
   \]
   makes every positive-index normalized term equal to \(\mu(x)\); hence its limiting/infimum construction is also \(\mu(x)\). The assumption \(\mu(1)\le1\) supplies the normalization required by the smoothing lemma.

4. Evaluation at a fixed \(x\) preserves finite suprema of seminorms. Thus
   \[
   \bigl(\sup_{i\in s}p_i\bigr)(x)=\max_{i\in s}p_i(x),
   \]
   and a maximum over the nonempty finite set \(s\) is attained by some \(i\in s\). Nonemptiness is essential only for producing such an index.

Finally, assemble the conjunction, defining each direction of each `Iff` from the independently established statement on its target side.
